episode.lensDescription: Examine complexity and tradeoffs. Surface the questions worth asking.
episode.broadcastScript:
Welcome to The Innovation Pulse from Innovating Higher Ed. It's Monday, March 9th.

When students start demanding to know which professors use A.I. in their courses, institutions face questions they weren't prepared to answer. At the University of Missouri, a student group is pushing for transparency that's driving policy changes campus-wide.

-
From our Beyond Ed category today, we're seeing community college athletics making headlines in East Texas. Mabank High School graduate Cayden Truelove drove in three runs as National Park College swept a doubleheader against Sauk Valley Community College. It's a nice reminder of how community colleges continue providing pathways for student athletes to extend their playing careers while pursuing their education.

-
Now, let's get to that story I mentioned at the top about students demanding A.I. transparency at Missouri.

At the University of Missouri, something interesting is happening that flips the usual narrative about A.I. resistance in higher education. A student organization called Students for Human Intelligence has been systematically emailing professors across campus with a straightforward question: How do you plan to implement A.I. in your classes?

The group wants transparency so students can make informed decisions about which courses to take. They're not asking professors to stop using A.I. entirely, but they want to know what they're signing up for when they register for a class. In response to this student pressure, the university's Faculty Council is now voting on a proposed A.I. policy that would require instructors to disclose their level of A.I. usage using a standardized scale.

This represents a fascinating shift in campus A.I. conversations. For the past two years, most discussions have centered on preventing student misuse of A.I. tools. Institutions have been crafting honor codes, updating academic integrity policies, and training faculty to detect A.I.-generated work. Now we're seeing students themselves organizing to push back against faculty use of A.I. in instruction and curriculum design. It's a reversal that catches many administrators off guard.

The Missouri situation highlights competing perspectives about A.I.'s role in education. Students for Human Intelligence argues that extensive A.I. use could "devalue all of our education" and that it's better to "keep things human." Meanwhile, faculty committee chair Kevin Brown frames the proposed disclosure system as being "proactive" and responsive to student needs while helping students "understand that we are listening to them."

What makes this particularly complex is the practical challenge it creates for institutions. Most faculty members are still figuring out how to thoughtfully integrate A.I. tools into their teaching. Being required to categorize and publicly disclose their A.I. usage level adds a layer of complexity that many weren't anticipating. It also raises questions about what constitutes "A.I. use" in instruction. Does using ChatGPT to brainstorm discussion questions count the same as having students analyze A.I.-generated content? What about using A.I. for administrative tasks like organizing course materials?

The Missouri approach involves creating a tiered disclosure system where faculty would indicate their level of A.I. integration. But this surfaces deeper questions about academic freedom and pedagogical choice. When students can effectively vote with their feet by avoiding courses with higher A.I. usage ratings, it creates market pressures that could influence curricular decisions in ways we haven't fully considered.

For community colleges, where we serve diverse student populations with varying comfort levels around technology, this kind of transparency demand could be particularly complex to navigate. Many of our students are already juggling work, family, and financial pressures. Adding A.I. usage levels as another factor in course selection decisions creates yet another layer of complexity in their educational planning.

The story also suggests that student attitudes about A.I. in education are more nuanced and varied than we might assume. Some students clearly want the option to choose courses with minimal A.I. integration. They may prefer traditional instruction methods or worry about A.I. diminishing their learning experience. Others may be comfortable with or even prefer more A.I.-enhanced instruction, seeing it as preparation for a workplace where these tools are increasingly common.

This creates a challenge for institutions trying to balance transparency with the pedagogical freedom faculty need to innovate and adapt their teaching methods. If a professor wants to experiment with A.I. tools to enhance student learning, should they have to publicly declare that experimentation in a way that might discourage enrollment?

The Missouri case also raises questions about who gets to determine appropriate levels of A.I. integration in higher education. Traditionally, these decisions have been made by faculty and academic departments based on pedagogical goals and learning outcomes. Now students are asserting their voice in these decisions, which isn't necessarily wrong, but it does represent a shift in how curricular choices get made.

What's particularly worth watching is how this plays out practically. Will courses with higher A.I. usage ratings see lower enrollment? Will faculty feel pressured to minimize their A.I. integration to avoid being labeled as less "human" in their teaching approach? Or will students actually appreciate the transparency and make more informed choices about their educational experience?

For those of us teaching Monday morning, this story matters because it suggests we need to think more carefully about how we communicate our pedagogical choices to students. Whether or not your institution adopts a formal disclosure system, being transparent about how and why you use various tools in your teaching can help students understand your approach and feel more confident in their learning experience.

-
The Missouri story reminds us that transparency often creates as many questions as it answers. How do we balance student agency with pedagogical innovation? That's your Innovation Pulse for Monday. Find full coverage and links at innovating higher ed dot com. See you Tuesday.
